title: Antibiotic resistance and the missing pipeline

turns.speaker: Colin
turns.text: There hasn't been a genuinely new class of antibiotic approved since the eighties. Not a variation. A new class.

turns.speaker: Drew
turns.text: That can't be for lack of trying.

turns.speaker: Yusra
turns.text: It's partly the science getting harder and mostly the economics being upside down. You develop a drug, and if it works the correct thing to do is not use it.

turns.speaker: Colin
turns.text: Keep it in reserve for the cases nothing else touches.

turns.speaker: Yusra
turns.text: Which means no sales. Every other drug rewards volume and this one punishes it.

turns.speaker: Drew
turns.text: So the companies left the field.

turns.speaker: Yusra
turns.text: Almost entirely. Several that did get one approved went bankrupt afterwards, which is not a story that attracts investors.

turns.speaker: Colin
turns.text: There are subscription models being tried. A health service pays a flat annual fee for access whether it prescribes any or not.

turns.speaker: Drew
turns.text: Paying for availability rather than by the box.

turns.speaker: Colin
turns.text: Exactly, and early results look reasonable, though the sums involved are small so far.

turns.speaker: Yusra
turns.text: The other half is agriculture. A large share of all antibiotics used go to livestock, often not to treat anything.

turns.speaker: Drew
turns.text: That seems easier to fix than inventing a drug class.

turns.speaker: Colin
turns.text: Easier technically. It's a farming cost, so it's a political problem instead.

points: No genuinely new class of antibiotic has been approved since the 1980s.
Yusra explains the economics are inverted: an effective new antibiotic should be held in reserve, so it generates no sales.
Companies have largely left the field, and several that gained approval went bankrupt afterwards.
Subscription models pay a flat fee for availability rather than per prescription, with modest early results.
A large share of antibiotics goes to livestock, often not to treat illness.
Colin notes agricultural use is technically easier to address but politically harder because it raises farming costs.
